spot: Open granite face on the Vertical Mile Challenge route

detail.reason: An ascending bare slab gaining ~350 ft with long sightlines, but it is a steep climbing face, not a summit/rim/overlook destination with a long view DOWN; the view is the summit at top, not here.
'Long open sightlines while ascending' = open vista, but it is a directional uphill view, not a broad summit panorama.
Open friction slab is the antithesis of a crevice/undercut/overhang; bare exposed rock offers no above-ground recess to tuck a box.
No digging on bare granite, but a slab gives nowhere natural to rest a box against (no ledge/shelf/hollow at the face itself).
The operative feature IS rock: a large exposed granite slab/outcrop is the host landmark.
The slab is a dry exposed face; the creek crossing is below/before it, not beside this spot.
Bare open rock surrounded by forest is a forest/open-rock interface, loosely fitting 'forest meets open ground.'
Directly on the marked Vertical Mile Challenge Trail, walkable on foot, no bushwhack.
Whole park is under 3 mi from Rocky Face Church Rd; reached in ~1-2 mi on foot, no water crossing/cliff scaling at this spot.
A large open exposed slab on a popular challenge route is the opposite of secluded/out-of-sight.
No gap/saddle/notch between paired crags; it is a single open slope.
Open bare rock; no prominent tree marker (flatrock specialists, not trees).
No documented eastern orientation; the slab climbs toward the summit, aspect not eastward in sources.
It is a granitic-dome face (exfoliating, broadly rounded), loosely echoing domed/rounded stone, but it is a slab not a discrete egg/dome boulder.
Dry rock moss and flatrock plants grow on the bare grey granite, giving green-on-stone contrast.
Host material is granitic gneiss — hard crystalline quartz/feldspar/mica-bearing rock with grit/glint.
Smooth friction slab, not angular/faceted/stratified/columnar rock.
Light-grey granite, but spring elf-orpine/flatrock mats add reddish tint and the open slab is sunlit; weak.
Broad bare light-grey granite slab standing pale against the surrounding dark forest.
Convex/flat slab, no bowl/basin/pit concavity at this spot.
No confluence or watercourse bend at the slab.
Approach crosses a creek (low point) then climbs to the high spot, a faint 'down-then-up' shape.
QR-code Vertical-Mile-Challenge signs are small man-made marks along the route, though they are signs not a natural seam/inscription.
Route turns RIGHT off Grindstone onto the Challenge trail; no left nudge here.
Large exposed slab fully open to wind/sun/rain, matching the breezy-exposed (not sealed cave) cue.
No fixed marker-to-spot pace count; the slab spans ~0.3 mi with no defined count point.
